In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional and morphological analysis of retinal cells in a mouse model of X-linked congenital night blindness type 1 (CSNB1) and X-linked congenital day blindness (CDRB).
the functional characterization of the IT mouse line as model for human X-linked congenital night blindness type 1.
the functional analysis of a novel mouse model for CSNB2 and its potential use for the development of new treatment strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IT mice are a good model to study the functional phenotype of CSNB patients with gain-of function mutations in the CACN1F gene.
the gain-of-function mutations result in a reduced dynamic range for the photoreceptor cells and therefore a reduced dynamic range in the visual system as a whole.

the I745T mutation causes a shift in the voltage-dependent activation curve, which leads to a reduction in the dynamic range of the photoreceptors, which is reflected in a reduction of the outer nuclear layer and the outer plexifrom layer, which leads to an impairment of vision in the IT mouse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IT mouse line represents a model for the functional and morphological phenotype of CSNB2 patients carrying a gain-of-function CACNA1 F mutation.
the IT mouse line is a suitable model for the functional consequences of human CSNB mutations in the CAC1AF gene and may help to understand the pathophysiological consequences of these mutations.
the IT mouse line is an appropriate model for CSNB2 patients carrying the gain-of-function mutations I745T or R1448Q in the Cav1. 4 channel.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we provide the first comprehensive description of a CSNB2 mouse line that allows for the investigation of pathophysiological mechanisms underlying CSNB2.
the IT mouse line serves a specific model for human CSNB2 and that it may help to further understanding of the pathophysiology in CSNB.
the IT mouse line is a suitable model for human CSNB2 with gain-of-function Cav1.4 channel mutations.
